demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette: Rohan's eyes still lingered on the rearview mirror, his mind replaying the accident that had changed everything. It had been a typical delivery route, but a split-second distraction - a glance at his phone to check the GPS - and he failed to notice the pedestrian stepping off the curb. The sound of screeching tires and crunching metal still haunted him. The image of the victim, a young woman, crumpling to the ground, her eyes wide with pain, seared into his memory. As he sat in the hospital waiting room, waiting for news on the woman's condition, Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that he was responsible for the accident. He kept thinking about what he could have done differently - if only he had been more attentive, if only he had taken a different route. The guilt began to gnaw at him, and he became convinced that he had failed to protect others, just as his parents had always taught him to do. "What kind of person am I," he thought, "that I couldn't even keep someone safe?" The days turned into weeks, and Rohan found himself becoming withdrawn. He stopped socializing with friends, stopped going out with his wife, Nalini. She tried to reassure him that it was an accident, that anyone could have been in his shoes, but he just couldn't shake off the feeling of self-blame. "If only I had acted differently," he'd tell himself, "none of this would have happened." He began to question every decision he made on the road - was he checking his mirrors enough? Was he following too closely? As a delivery driver, Rohan's job required him to be on the road for hours at a stretch. But now, every drive became an ordeal. He'd find himself scanning the sidewalks, anticipating potential hazards, and braking suddenly at the slightest sign of movement. His anxiety began to affect his work - he started getting complaints from customers about delayed deliveries, and his supervisor called him in for a talk. Nalini tried to be supportive, but Rohan's withdrawal was taking a toll on their relationship. She'd try to initiate conversations, but he'd just shrug her off, feeling like he didn't deserve her comfort. He began to feel like a burden, like he was failing his wife and himself. The guilt and self-blame had become all-consuming. One day, as Rohan was driving home from work, he saw an accident on the side of the road - a car had hit a pedestrian, just like in his own accident. His heart racing, Rohan pulled over, feeling an overwhelming urge to get out and help. But something held him back - fear of being reminded of his own failure? Fear of not knowing what to do? He sat there, frozen, as other people rushed to the victim's aid. It was then that Rohan realized he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this - trapped in a cycle of guilt and self-blame. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find some way to forgive himself and learn to live with what had happened. As he sat in the waiting room, clutching his wife's hand, Rohan knew it wouldn't be easy. But for the first time in months, he felt a glimmer of hope - maybe, just maybe, he could learn to see himself as more than just a failure.
